en: The Treatise on Dependent Origination,
composed by the Noble Ullangha;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of South India during the Great Sui Dynasty.
From one arises three; from three, six are produced.
From six and two, again six arise; from six, further six are born.
From six there are three; these three, in turn, have three more.
The three arise again from the four, and the four arise again from the three.
From the three they arise as one, and that one arises again as seven;
whatever suffering exists therein, the Muni has declared it all to be included.
These twelvefold distinctions are taught as the "emptiness" of the perfectly pure;
because they arise through the power of dependent origination, one should understand these twelve factors.
Ignorance, karma, and consciousness, as well as name-and-form, the sense faculties, and the triad of contact, [feeling, craving, and grasping], [existence, birth, and aging-and-death].
Knowing thirst and grasping, as well as origination, cessation, ripening,
and the subsequent limit; the first, eighth, and ninth are afflictions, the second and tenth are karma,
and the remaining seven are all suffering— these three encompass the twelve factors.
The first two belong to the past, the latter two to the future, and the remaining eight to the present; this is called the Dharma of the Three Times.
Afflictions give rise to karma, which brings about retribution; from retribution, afflictions arise once more.
Afflictions give rise again to karma, and from karma there is likewise retribution.
If one is free from affliction, how could there be karma?
When karma is destroyed, there is likewise no retribution.
Without retribution, there is freedom from affliction; these three each cease of themselves.
The five factors that produce results are called the karmas of affliction;
the seven factors are taken as the results—these seven kinds of suffering should be kept in mind.
Within the cause, the fruit is empty; within the cause, the cause is also absent.
Within the fruit, the cause is empty; within the fruit, the fruit is also absent.
Both cause and fruit are empty; the wise one accords with this.
In the world there are four kinds of divisions; they exist because cause and fruit are combined.
When afflictions, karma, and fruit are combined, and with the addition of desire and mindfulness, they form six divisions.
Because they are subsumed within sections, there are two sections and three summaries.
The causes and effects are combined into sections; the third and fourth sections are summarized and abbreviated.
[The sequence is] two, two, three, three, two. During the time of suffering there are five factors:
the agent, the womb, the objective field, the initiation, and the transformation of the flow.
The fruit of the arousal of delusion and the two fruits of retribution and outflow constitute [the first category];
within the factors of the associated faculties, each has three or two parts.
The fruits of feverish affliction and poverty, and the fruits of emergence and flowing forth, [constitute the second].
Within the section on "Conjunction with Others," there are two, one, one, and one dharma.
These consist of twelve kinds; they arise from conditions of equal power and from themselves.
There is no sentient being and no life-principle; they are without motion, to be known through wisdom.
There is no self and nothing belonging to a self; there is no self and no cause for a self.
These four kinds of non-knowledge are empty, and the remaining parts are likewise so.
Free from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism—this is precisely the Middle Way.
If awakening is fully accomplished, the essence of awakening is the Buddhas.
Having awakened, amidst the assembly, the Sage and Holy One taught non-self;
in the *Nagaropama-sūtra*, the Guide explained this meaning.
The Kātyāyanasūtra states that both right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and the view of emptiness (*śūnyatādṛṣṭi*) are taught;
furthermore, the Pārāyaṇa-sūtra—so named after the lunar mansion *Kṛttikā*—also speaks of a particularly distinguished emptiness.
One who knows the correspondence with emptiness, yet does not understand dependent origination, does not understand that emptiness.
Thus, one does not grow weary of the aggregates;
if one holds such views, they are views of existence and non-existence.
Thus, one who understands the meaning of dependent origination and is free from pride realizes emptiness; because they also cultivate revulsion toward the aggregates of sensation,
they do not become confused regarding the convergence of karma and its fruit.
Nor is it not conditioned by this; through emptiness as a condition, there exist these requisites for experiencing karmic retribution.
The dependent origination has already been explained previously: those afflictions, karma, and suffering.
From the three, as they accord with the Dharma, the two arise;
from the two, the seven are produced; and from the seven, the three are again produced.
Thus the wheel of existence revolves.
There are no sentient beings existing apart from this;
it is only within empty phenomena that empty phenomena arise from themselves.
Relying on conditions, karma is produced; relying on conditions, retribution is likewise produced.
There is not one that does not have conditions:
sunlight, seeds, and sourness; the various continuities do not transcend these.
Wisdom should contemplate those two.
The Root Text of the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* on Dependent Origination is complete. I shall now provide an explanatory commentary following its sequence:
From one, three arise; From three, six are produced;
From six, two, two, and again six; And from six, six are likewise born.

Regarding "one gives rise to three": the first refers to non-knowledge (*ajñāna*). This non-knowledge is termed ignorance (*avidyā*); because one does not realize suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, it is called non-knowledge.

Due to ignorance, there arise what are called the three types of formations—meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable—as well as bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations, which are produced from them.

Regarding "from the three, six arise": from those three formations, the six groups of consciousness arise, namely: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
"Six from two" means that those six groups of consciousness arise from two things, namely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

"Two further give rise to six" means that the two types, name-and-form, further give rise to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), namely: the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.

"From the six, the six also arise" means that from those six sense bases (āyatana), the six types of contact (sparśa) are produced in turn: namely, eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.
From the six [bases] there arise the three; these three again give rise to three;
from those three, four are produced; and from those four, three are produced again.

Regarding "from the six there arise the three": from those six contacts (sparśa), three feelings (vedanā) are further produced—namely, pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Regarding these three, there are again three types: from those three feelings, three kinds of craving arise in turn, namely, craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmatṛṣṇā*), craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).

Regarding "the three further give rise to the four": from those three types of craving, the four graspings (upādāna) are produced in turn—namely, the grasping for sense-pleasures (kāmopādāna), the grasping for views (dṛṣṭyupādāna), the grasping for rules and rituals (śīlavratopādāna), and the grasping for the doctrine of self (ātmavādopādāna).

From the four, three further arise; from those four graspings (*upādāna*), the three realms of existence (*bhava*)—namely, the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)—are produced in turn.
From the three, one arises; from that one, seven further arise.
All the suffering contained therein is said by the Muni to be fully encompassed.
Regarding "from three, one arises": by taking those same three existences as conditions, one type of birth in the future arises.
Regarding "that one further gives rise to seven": from that single [birth], there further arise the seven types consisting of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, affliction, and despair.

Regarding the statement that "all suffering therein is said by the Muni to be subsumed [within this]": beginning with ignorance and ending with exhaustion, the immeasurable varieties of suffering briefly described by the Blessed One are all subsumed herein.
The twelvefold distinctions are explained as being perfectly pure emptiness;
because of the power of the factors of dependent origination, one should understand these twelve dharmas.

Regarding the statement that "the twelvefold distinctions are explained as being perfectly pure emptiness": this refers to the fact that ignorance and the other factors are each distinct and unmixed, thus constituting twelve branches.

Furthermore, all these are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). One should correctly perceive that what has been thus described consists solely of empty phenomena and self-arisen empty phenomena.

Regarding the statement "one should know the twelve factors by virtue of the power of the divisions of dependent origination": if one considers them by way of the power of the sequential divisions of arising, those twelve factors should be understood as follows: therein, the characteristic of delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*);
at the stage of formative action (*saṃskāra*), the accumulation of the characteristics of future existence is volitional formation (*saṃskāra*).
In that section on consciousness, the characteristic of the subsequent emergence of the factors of rebirth is consciousness;
in that section on name-and-form, the characteristic of the integration of the mental body and the physical body is name-and-form;
in that section on the six sense bases, the characteristic of the establishment of the [sensory] modalities is the six sense bases.
Regarding the category of contact (*sparśa*): that which is the coming together and mutual interaction of the eye, forms, and consciousness is contact.
Regarding the category of feeling (*vedanā*): that which is characterized by the experience of the pleasant and the unpleasant is feeling.
Regarding the category of craving (*tṛṣṇā*): that which is characterized by lack of contentment is craving.
That which, in the context of the category of grasping (*upādāna*), consists of the characteristics of seizing and appropriating is grasping;
that which, in the context of the category of existence (*bhava*), consists of the characteristics of the name-body (*nāmakāya*) and the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is existence;
that which, in the context of the category of arising (*jāti*), consists of the characteristics of the production of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is arising.
In the context of the category of aging, that which has the characteristic of maturation is aging;
in the context of the category of death, that which is the severance of the life-faculty is death;
in the context of the category of sorrow, that which has the characteristic of exaltation is sorrow.
In the context of the term "sorrow" (*śoka*), that which is the sound of weeping is sorrow;
in the context of the term "suffering" (*duḥkha*), the characteristic of the body being scorched and heated is suffering;
in the context of the term "affliction" (*upāyāsa*), the characteristic of the mind being oppressed and distressed is affliction.
That which is the state of being exhausted and the sign of extreme fatigue is "exhaustion" (pariḷāha).
Ignorance, karma, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling,
craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death constitute the arising, the emergence, the ripening, and the final limit [of suffering].
Among these, that which lacks wisdom is ignorance (*avidyā*);
action (*karman*) is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*);
and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is discernment (*prajñapti*).
Name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is the aggregate collection of the five aggregates (skandha).
The sense faculties (indriya) are the bases (āyatana).
The coming together of the three is contact (sparśa).
"Knowing" refers to sensation;
"thirsting" refers to craving;
and "grasping" refers to clinging.
Accumulation is existence;
emergence is birth;
ripening is old age.
The "final limit" refers to death.
Furthermore, I shall now explain in sequence how these various distinctions are subsumed.
Among them, there are the distinctions of karma, afflictions, and retribution:
The first, eighth, and ninth are afflictions; the second and tenth are karma;
the remaining seven are all suffering. These three categories encompass the twelve factors.
As for the three afflictions: ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
The two karmas are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*).

The seven results of retribution are consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
These twelve factors are subsumed under three categories.
Furthermore, in terms of temporal distinction:
the first two belong to the past, and the latter two belong to the future.
The remaining eight belong to the present; these are called the factors of the three times.
Ignorance and formations are the first two types, belonging to the past time.
Birth and old age and death are the latter two types, belonging to the future time.
Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, and becoming—these eight factors exist in the present time;
furthermore, each of these arises sequentially from the preceding one.
Afflictions give rise to karma, which brings about retribution;
retribution in turn gives rise to afflictions, and afflictions again give rise to karma.

Furthermore, retribution exists because of karma. The three types—affliction, karma, and retribution—are as previously explained: because of those afflictions there is karma; because of karma there is retribution; again, because of retribution there are afflictions; because of afflictions there is karma; and because of karma there is retribution.
Question: Regarding the statement that through the exhaustion of afflictions there is individual cessation—
what is the meaning of this?
The answer is:
Apart from affliction, how could there be karma? When karma is destroyed, there is no retribution;
when there is no retribution, one is free from affliction. These three each cease of their own accord.

If this mind is free from the defilement of afflictions, one does not accumulate karma; if one does not perform karma, one does not undergo retribution; and if retribution is extinguished, afflictions will likewise not arise.
Thus, these three each cease of their own accord.
Furthermore, these possess the divisions of cause and effect:
the five factors that produce an effect are called afflictions and karma.
Seven parts constitute the fruit; one should contemplate the seven kinds of suffering.

The five kinds of causes are termed afflictions and karma; they are as previously explained: ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*).

As for the arising of the sevenfold fruit, it is also as previously described regarding the sevenfold suffering, namely: consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and old age and death.
Furthermore, these two types of emptiness regarding cause and effect are as follows:
within the cause there is no effect, and within the cause there is also no cause;
within the effect there is no cause, and within the effect there is also no effect.
Both cause and effect are empty; the wise one accords with this.
In the Sanskrit original, there was but one verse, which is now rendered as one and a half verses.
Regarding these two types—cause and effect—as described here: if the cause is empty, the effect is also empty; if the effect is empty, the cause is also empty.
Thus, the cause is an empty cause, and the fruit is an empty fruit.
One should accord with these four limits.
Furthermore, there is another division of this.
The fourfold division within the world exists through the conjunction of cause and effect;
the conjunction of afflictions, karma, and fruit, with the desire for mindfulness as the sixth division.

Regarding "the fourfold division within the world exists through the conjunction of cause and effect": because the five kinds of causes and seven kinds of fruits within the path are combined, they are summarized briefly into four types, which sequentially constitute the fourfold division.
Among these, ignorance and formations constitute the first portion during the past time;
consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling constitute the second portion during the present time.
Thirst, craving, grasping, and becoming also belong to the present time and constitute the third part.
Birth and old age and death belong to the future time and constitute the fourth part, consisting of two factors.
This refers to the four types of divisions.

Regarding the six divisions consisting of the conjunction of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and fruit (*vipāka*) with craving (*tṛṣṇā*): through the combination of the three types—affliction, karma, and retribution—and by way of their sequential order, there are six divisions within the two fundamental [categories].
Among these, from ignorance up to feeling, ignorance is the root.
From craving up to old age and death, craving is the root.

Within the root of ignorance, ignorance constitutes the affliction portion; volitional formations constitute the karma portion; and consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling constitute the retribution portion.

Within the roots of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), craving and grasping (*upādāna*) belong to the category of afflictions (*kleśa*); existence (*bhava*) belongs to the category of karma; and birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) belong to the category of retribution (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, this is a concise summary of the divisions of the links (*aṅga*).
Because they are comprised within "sections" (*saṃdhāna*), there are two sections and three summaries;
cause and effect are combined as sections, while the third and fourth are general summaries.

Taking the "existence-section" (*bhava-saṃdhāna*) as the basis, two sections are initiated: namely, the interval between existence and birth is the first section, and the interval between formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the second section; these two together constitute the section of karmic fruit.
The third section consists of the conflation of cause and effect within sensation (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
These three sections are further condensed into four general summaries:

ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) constitute the first summary; consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and sensation (*vedanā*) constitute the second summary; craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) constitute the third summary; and birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) constitute the fourth summary.
This refers to the three sections and the four summaries.
Furthermore, regarding the distinctions in the duration of abiding within these dharmas:
two, two, three, three, and two; there are five dharmas during the time of suffering.
The author says: "The realm of the womb, / Arising, turning, and flowing forth.
Regarding the "pairs of dharmas": ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are said to be two kinds; consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are said to be two kinds.

Regarding the "three sets of three": the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are taught as one set of three; craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) are taught as another set of three.
Furthermore, regarding the "two": birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are taught as two.
These five factors—namely, the agent, the womb, the objective field, the activation, and the birth—circulate therein; they should be understood according to their respective numbers.
Among these, ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) should be viewed as the agent during the time of suffering;
consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) should be viewed as the embryo during the time of suffering.
The three factors of the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are said to be the objects within the period of suffering.
Craving, grasping, and existence are said to be the activities that arise and proceed within the period of suffering.
Birth and old age and death—these two types are said to arise within the midst of suffering.
Furthermore, there is the differentiation of results:
the result of the arousal of delusion and the result of the flow of retribution constitute these two.
Within the section on the corresponding faculties (*indriya*), each consists of three or two parts.

As previously stated, regarding these roots of ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*): within the first part of the root of ignorance, one is deluded and gives rise to the flow of retribution (*vipākasaṃtati*), which is termed the four kinds of fruits.
Within each of these groups of three and two, they should be understood as corresponding according to their respective order.

Among them, ignorance is the fruit of delusion; volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the fruit of origination; consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases are the fruit of retribution; and contact and sensation are the fruit of flux.
Furthermore, there are other residual fruits:
the fruit of burning affliction and poverty, the fruit of flowing forth from transformation,
and those associated with the portions of others— namely, two, one, one, and one dharma respectively.

As previously explained in the second section on the roots of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), regarding the arising of the fruits such as feverish distress (*paridāha*) and poverty (*vaikalya*), these should be applied accordingly to each respective category within this teaching.
Among these, craving and grasping are the fruit of feverish affliction; becoming is the fruit of poverty; birth is the fruit of emergence; and old age and death are the fruit of the outflow.
Thus, these constitute eight fruits.
These are of twelve kinds, arising spontaneously through the power of equal conditions;
they are without a sentient being and without a life-principle, and are known through wisdom as being without movement.

Thus, beginning with ignorance and ending with old age and death, there are twelve links; because they are equally supreme, each arises in dependence upon the others. Yet, there is no sentient being, no life-span, and no agent—this should be understood through wisdom.
In this, there are no sentient beings because they are not solid;
there is no life-span because there is no self;
there is no agent because there is no doer.
There is no self and nothing belonging to a self; there is no self and no cause of a self.
These four kinds of non-knowledge are empty, and the remaining parts are likewise so.

Regarding the absence of self, there is non-knowledge; regarding the absence of what belongs to a self, there is non-knowledge; regarding the absence of a self, there is non-knowledge; and regarding the absence of the cause of a self, there is non-knowledge. Because of this absence of self, these four kinds of non-knowledge are empty.
Just as the fourfold sequence is empty of ignorance, so too should one know that the remaining factors, such as the practice [of the path], are all empty.
Free from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, this is itself the Middle Way;
when awakening is fully accomplished, the essence of that awakening is the Buddhas.

Existence is subsumed under permanence, and non-existence is subsumed under annihilation; these two extremes serve as conditions, and from them, various forms of existence arise in this and that place.

To depart from these two extremes is the Middle Way. Those ignorant non-Buddhists fall into the extremes, whereas the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who have attained awakening, constitute the very essence of awakening.
In this world, he alone has achieved this; no other person possesses such a meaning.
Having awakened, the Sage spoke of non-self among the assembly;
in the *Nagaropama-sūtra*, the Guide explained this very principle.
Having awakened to this Middle Way therein, the Buddha taught non-self among the masses.
That is to say, monks!
Those who possess the notions of "self" and "mine"—the childish, ordinary worldlings who lack learning—follow and fall into conventional designations.
Within this, there is no longer "I" or "mine.
Monks! At the time of arising, it is merely suffering that arises; at the time of ceasing, it is merely suffering that ceases.
As the Teacher has already explained this meaning in the *Sūtra of the Simile of the City*.
Furthermore, the *Kātyāyanāvavāda-sūtra* states: "Right view and the view of emptiness—"
The *Prakaraṇapāda-sūtra* is the name of the constellation Aśvinī; it also speaks of the supreme emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
These three sūtras and others likewise describe such characteristics, which the Blessed One has already taught; those [teachings] are also this very same thing.
If one correctly understands dependent origination, one knows it as being conjoined with emptiness;
if one does not understand dependent origination, one likewise does not know that emptiness.
Regarding the aforementioned dependent origination, if there is correct understanding, that knowledge is no different [from the realization of emptiness].
What, moreover, does he know?
It is that he knows emptiness.

If one does not understand dependent origination, one will also not understand its emptiness; if one does not understand this dependent origination, one will likewise be unable to comprehend and enter into that emptiness.
One should know this:
if one gives rise to conceit regarding emptiness, one will not grow weary of the multitude of aggregates;
if one holds to the view of non-existence, one will be deluded concerning the meaning of dependent origination.

"If one gives rise to conceit regarding emptiness, one will not feel weary of the five aggregates of clinging": if one gives rise to conceit regarding emptiness, one will not produce weariness and detachment toward the five aggregates of clinging.

"If one possesses that view of non-existence, one is deluded regarding the meaning of dependent origination": furthermore, because one is deluded regarding this meaning of dependent origination due to the view of non-existence, one will adopt whichever of the four views is taken: first, the view of nihilism; second, the view of eternalism; third, the doctrine of creation by a Sovereign Lord (*īśvara*); and fourth, the doctrine that [all things] depend solely upon what was done in previous lives.
Because they are not deluded regarding dependent origination, they abandon conceit and realize emptiness;
because they are weary of the multitude of sensations, they are not deluded regarding the convergence of karma and its results.

Regarding the line "Because they are not deluded regarding dependent origination, they abandon conceit and realize emptiness": if one is without a deluded mind concerning the various instances of dependent origination previously explained, and if one attains the abandonment of conceit regarding the grasping of "self" and "what belongs to self," then one is able to enter into emptiness in accordance with the Dharma.

Regarding the statement that one does not become deluded concerning the convergence of karma and its fruits because of weariness with the aggregates of grasping: because one grasps at "self" and "what belongs to self" within the five aggregates of grasping, one revolves through the world incessantly;
however, by giving rise to revulsion and detachment toward those aggregates of grasping, one will then be free from inversion and confusion regarding the continuity of this karma and its fruits.
He asked again:
"What is the meaning of this?
Karma acts as a condition for the continuity of birth, yet it is not that there is no such condition."
"Emptiness as a condition must have this: it is the equipment for receiving karmic retribution.

Karma acts as a condition for the continuity of birth, nor is it that there is no such conditioning. Regarding the defilement of afflictions and karma as previously explained, by means of such pure and impure karma, sentient beings are propelled and born in a continuous succession across the horizontal, upward, and downward realms.
If it were not for this karma, it would not function as a condition.

If this were not the case, then there would be the arrival [of results] before the action is completed, and the loss [of results] once the action is completed. "Arrival" refers to the result arriving even though the action has not yet been completed; "loss" refers to the result being lost once the action has already been completed.

Regarding the statement that there must be these karmic retributions and requisites for enjoyment conditioned by emptiness: if there is the experience of retribution from such pure and impure karma, then its intrinsic nature is empty.
Fundamentally there is no self; it arises through conditions, and one should likewise know that its intrinsic nature is empty.
To further explain this meaning briefly:
the twelvefold classification, previously explained as dependent origination, [is as follows].
Those afflictions, karma, and suffering are subsumed within these three categories according to the Dharma.
Ignorance is the beginning and old age and death are the end; this is the differentiation of the twelve links of dependent origination, as previously explained.
Among those, three are afflictions, two are karma, and seven are suffering; all are thus subsumed.
From the three, the two arise; from the two, the seven arise;
and from the seven, the three arise again. Thus does the wheel of existence revolve.

The two types of formations produced by the three factors of ignorance, craving, and grasping, and the seven factors produced by those two—namely, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and old age and death.
Within those seven factors, as previously explained, three types arise again; from those three, two arise once more; and from those two, seven arise yet again.
Thus, these two types proceed in succession without interruption, and this wheel of existence (bhava-cakra) revolves in this manner throughout.
In the world where causes and effects arise, there is no separate sentient being;
it is only within empty phenomena that empty phenomena themselves arise.

Regarding "in the world where causes and effects arise, there is no separate sentient being": ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are the five factors termed "causes. Consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are the seven factors termed "effects. All of these pervade the world.

Whether it be the self, or sentient beings, or life-span, or the one who is born, or the person, or the individual, or the agent—know that these, taken as primary and distinguished in succession, are nothing but deceptive illusions.
How do they arise?

It is simply that from empty phenomena, empty phenomena themselves arise; that is to say, within the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), afflictions, karma, and results are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*). It is only from distinct empty phenomena that the conventionally designated phenomena of afflictions, karma, and results arise.
This is its meaning:
Dependent on conditions, afflictions arise; dependent on conditions, karma also arises;
dependent on conditions, retribution also arises; there is not a single thing that does not have conditions.
If there are afflictions, then there are various and immeasurable kinds of karma, as well as the various fruits of retribution produced by that karma.
One should know that these all share common causes and common conditions.
There is not a single place that exists without causes and conditions.
Furthermore, to clarify this meaning, I shall now provide further analogies:
recitation, lamps, seals, mirrors, sounds, sunlight, seeds, and fermented vinegar.
The multitude of continuities does not transcend [the duality]; wisdom should contemplate those two.
As it is said in recitation: there is the teacher who recites and the student who receives the recitation; that which the teacher recites does not reach the one who receives it.
Why is this? Because the one who teaches the recitation still remains established [in that state],
and thus the teaching and the recitation do not form a continuous succession.
Why is this? Because it does not arise from itself.
Just as a lamp arises in succession, it is not that the first lamp leaps directly to the next, nor is it that the second arises without a cause.

In this way, these pairs—the seal and its image, the face and the mirror, the sound and its echo, the sun and fire, the seed and the sprout, and the sour taste and the saliva on the tongue—all of these do not transcend [one another], yet they are not non-arising, nor do they arise without a cause.

When those two kinds of five aggregates continue in succession until they reach [the next state], it is not that the first set of aggregates leaps over to the next; nor is the second set of aggregates something that does not arise, nor does it arise without a cause.
The wise person should correctly contemplate how these sensations continue in succession without skipping over, reaching their destination in due order.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of internal and external experiences, all of which should be observed.

Regarding the ten kinds [of characteristics] within and without: first, because it is impermanent; second, because it is not annihilated; third, because it does not transcend [to another state]; fourth, because there is no interval; fifth, because it is not that entity itself; sixth, because it is not something distinct; seventh, because there is no agent; eighth, because it is not without cause; ninth, because it is empty in every moment; and tenth, because it is bound by the characteristics of homogeneous effects.

Because all external seeds have been extinguished without remainder, yet the sprout does not arise eternally; because the seed has been extinguished without remainder, yet the sprout—which previously did not exist—now arises, it does not transcend [the principle of dependent origination].
That which constitutes the continuity is without interruption; because cause and effect are linked, there is no interval between them.

Because of the distinction between seed and sprout, it is not identical to that [seed]; because it arises from that, it is not something separate. Because of the conjunction of causes and conditions, there is no agent; because the seed serves as the cause, it is not without a cause.
Because seeds, sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth arise in succession from one another, they are empty moment by moment.
Since sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent results emerge according to the distinctions of their causes, the characteristics of similar results are interconnected therein.
Regarding the ten internal [characteristics]: first, because the collection of aggregates at the limit of death ceases without remainder, it is impermanent;
second, because one obtains the collection of aggregates for the subsequent birth, it is not annihilated;

third, once the collection of aggregates at the limit of death has ceased without remainder, the collection of aggregates for the subsequent birth arises where there was previously nothing—thus, it does not involve a transmigration.
Fourth, because the continuum of the aggregates of experience undergoes no interruption and cause and effect are linked, there is no interval between them;
fifth, because the aggregates of experience at the moment of death differ from those of the subsequent birth-moment, they do not possess the same substance;
sixth, because the latter arises from the former, they are not distinct entities.
Seventh, because they arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, there is no creator;
eighth, because afflictions and karma serve as their causes, they are not without cause;

ninth, because they are produced through a continuous succession of stages—namely, the kalala, arbuda, peśī, ghana, āsya, birth from the womb, infancy, childhood, youth, and old age—they are empty in every moment.
Tenth, through the perfuming of the wholesome and the unwholesome, the fruit evolves according to the distinctions of its causes; therefore, the fruits of a similar kind are mutually connected.
Furthermore, there are three verses:
Just as the flame of a lamp arises in succession, The collection of consciousnesses is likewise.
In the prior limit and the subsequent limit, there is likewise no accumulation.
There is non-arising and yet arising; through destruction, there is freedom from attachment.
Having arisen, there is no abiding, yet this activity continues to evolve.
If one can contemplate and know that what arises from those conditions is empty,
and establishes the teaching for its sake, that too is the Middle Way.
Within this, ignorance, volitional formations, craving, grasping, and existence constitute the Truth of Origination.
Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and old age and death—these constitute the truth of suffering.
The cessation of these twelve factors constitutes the truth of cessation.
If one can know dependent origination as it truly is, this is the Truth of the Path. *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhanganirdeśa* (Exposition of the Analysis of Dependent Origination and Other Topics).
